sonnet.problem: The card says the first eagle IS the king of Babylon and the topmost shoot IS Jerusalem's king and officials. Verse 12 explains events but never says outright that the eagle or the shoot stands for them. The card also cites only 17:12.
sonnet.rule: Leave open what the text leaves open. Who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect. This includes what a picture means. He retells the picture as the text gives it and says what it stands for only when the passage says so.

sonnet.problem: The card says the member of the royal family IS the seed the eagle planted. Verse 13 never says the seed stands for him, so the card connects the picture to its meaning without a verse that says so.
sonnet.rule: He says two names mean the same person only when a verse says so outright, and he gives that verse.

sonnet.problem: The question already says the seed is planted "by abundant waters." That rules out "dry" and makes "rocky" implausible, so the setup narrows the wrong answers.
sonnet.rule: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

sonnet.problem: The blank sits inside a direct quote of verse 20. The baker has not seen the line, so the card asks them to guess a word in it. The wrong answers "tent" and "cloak" make the choice a wording guess rather than a question about meaning.
sonnet.rule: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.
